subject: science
title: Forces and motion: why things move
intro: Why does a ball roll to a stop? Why are you pushed back into your seat when a car speeds up? The answers come from a few simple ideas about forces. A force is just a push or a pull, and once you understand how forces add up and change motion, a huge amount of everyday physics falls into place.

sections.heading: A force is a push or a pull
body: A **force** is a push or a pull on an object, measured in **newtons (N)**. Forces have a size and a direction — pushing a door and pulling it are different because the direction is different. Gravity pulling you down, friction slowing a slide, and your hand pushing a trolley are all forces.

Forces are drawn as arrows: longer arrow means bigger force, and the arrow points the way the force acts. Getting into the habit of drawing the forces on an object is the single best way to understand a physics problem.

sections.heading: Balanced and unbalanced forces
body: Usually more than one force acts on an object at once, and what matters is how they add up. When forces are **balanced** — equal and opposite — they cancel out, and the object either stays still or keeps moving steadily. A book resting on a table has gravity pulling down and the table pushing up, exactly balanced, so it stays put.

When forces are **unbalanced**, there's a leftover force in one direction, and *that* changes the motion: it speeds the object up, slows it down, or changes its direction. No change in motion means the forces are balanced; any change means they're not.

example.problem: A sled is pushed with 30 N forwards while friction pushes 10 N backwards. What is the overall force, and what happens?
steps: The forces are in opposite directions, so subtract: 30 N − 10 N = 20 N.
There is a leftover 20 N forwards, so the forces are unbalanced.
An unbalanced force in the forward direction speeds the sled up.
example.answer: A resultant force of 20 N forwards, so the sled accelerates forwards.

sections.heading: Three big rules (Newton's laws, in plain words)
body: **First:** an object keeps doing what it's doing — staying still, or moving steadily in a straight line — unless an unbalanced force acts on it. This is why a rolling ball only stops because friction pushes against it, and why you lurch forward when a car brakes: your body 'wants' to keep moving.

**Second:** the bigger the unbalanced force, the more an object speeds up — and heavier objects are harder to get moving. A hard push accelerates a trolley more than a gentle one, and an empty trolley is easier to accelerate than a full one.

**Third:** every force comes in a pair. When you push on something, it pushes back on you just as hard, the opposite way. A swimmer pushes water backwards, and the water pushes the swimmer forwards; a rocket pushes gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up.

sections.heading: Friction and gravity
body: **Friction** is a force that acts whenever surfaces rub, always pushing *against* motion. It's why a ball rolls to a stop and why you can walk without slipping. Friction can be a nuisance (slowing machines) or essential (brakes, grip) — it's not 'bad', just a force to account for.

**Gravity** is the pull between masses; on Earth it pulls everything toward the ground, giving objects their **weight**. Weight is a force (in newtons) and is different from mass (how much stuff is in an object). The same object has the same mass on the Moon but weighs less there, because the Moon's gravity is weaker.

options: A push or a pull on an object
The weight of an object only
practice.explain: A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons, with both a size and a direction.

practice.q: A book sits still on a table. What is true about the forces on it?
practice.explain: Gravity pulls it down and the table pushes up with an equal force — balanced forces, so it stays still.

practice.q: What does an unbalanced force do to an object?
options: Keeps it moving at constant speed
practice.explain: An unbalanced (leftover) force changes motion — speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction.

practice.q: A rolling ball slows down and stops. Which force is responsible?
practice.explain: Friction acts against the motion of the ball, gradually slowing it until it stops.

practice.q: You push on a wall and it doesn't move. According to Newton's third law, the wall:
options: Pushes back on you just as hard
practice.explain: Every force has an equal and opposite pair, so the wall pushes back on your hand with the same force you push with.

summary: A force is a push or a pull (in newtons) with a size and a direction — draw them as arrows.
Balanced forces cancel, so motion doesn't change; unbalanced forces change speed or direction.
Newton's ideas: objects keep doing what they're doing unless a force acts; bigger force means more acceleration; every force has an equal, opposite pair.
Friction always opposes motion, and gravity gives objects their weight (a force, different from mass).
